Hi,
I already have some agents in my Theia app, each with its own registered tools. In our setup, we use the Orchestrator as the default agent, so if the user does not specify which agent to use, the Orchestrator agent can select the best agent for the user's prompt.
Since Theia now has several ways to provide a custom system prompt to the agent (prompttemplate file or skill file), this sometimes leads to confusion about which to use.
My questions are:
1. What is the best practice for using these custom prompts?


(assume that there is no need to give each agent/prompt a different model; they can all use the same model)


a. As I have now: specific agents with their tools.


b. One master agent, with all other agents moved to skills that the master agent knows about and can choose from (in this case, the tools can be defined in each skill where needed).


c. Same as b, but using prompttemplate files instead of skills.

2. What is the difference between prompttemplate and skill in Theia?


(In both, we can set available variables and tools)


a. What are the capabilities of each?


b. When to use each?

Great questions and honestly, this is an area where things are moving incredibly fast and there's no single "right answer." Let me try to shed some light on the different mechanisms.
## Prompt Templates vs. Skills
The difference is more technical/historical than conceptual. We've had prompt templates (`.prompttemplate` files) in Theia AI for about 1.5 years now. Skills (SKILL.md) were released more recently as an emerging standard across AI coding tools. We support skills specifically to allow users to leverage existing skills from that ecosystem. One notable difference though: agents are capable of loading skills **on demand**, which helps keep the context window lean until a skill is actually needed.
## The Full Picture Is Even More Complex
In terms of what you can actually do to structure your AI setup, there are several mechanisms and they can be combined:
**a) Orchestrator routing:** The Orchestrator agent analyzes the user's request and routes it to the best-fitting agent. Importantly, the Orchestrator delegates the **full session** to the selected agent — once routed, the user stays with that agent for the remainder of the conversation. In our experience, results with this approach have been mixed. It tends to hide the existence of different agents from the user, which becomes problematic especially when agent capabilities are closely related to each other.
**b) Agent-to-agent delegation:** In contrast to the Orchestrator, this only delegates a **single step** to a sub-agent for a specific aspect, not the whole session. The key advantage is that everything happening in the delegation does **not** pollute the context of the main session — it's a clean delegation with defined input and output, and the sub-agent can have its own separate set of tools. Example: a GitHub agent can handle a GitHub-related action (collect info, create a PR, etc.) and return only the result to the main agent.
**c) User-driven extension:** Users can extend agents themselves with skills, prompt fragments, tools (including MCP servers), or slash commands — giving them control over what capabilities are available.
**d) Capabilities (since 1.69):** We now offer a way to encapsulate the various technical extension mechanisms into a user-visible concept. So instead of the user having to "activate delegation to the GitHub agent," it simply becomes "Activate GitHub." This abstracts the underlying technical approach into something more intuitive.
## Practical Guidance
As I said, there's no clear-cut answer on which approach works best — it depends on many factors: what are the use cases, how large are the base prompts, how complex is the task, etc. But in our experience from various projects, it helps to consider the following **key tradeoff**:
**Precision vs. usability without being explicit**
The more reduced and focused an agent's capabilities are, the better it usually performs. However, this makes orchestration harder and potentially requires the user to understand which agent to use or which capability to enable.
So as a practical starting point:
- If the task is **simple** and you have a **strong model**, you might just get away with **one agent** that has everything it needs.
- Rather than using the original Orchestrator model have a super agent that is capable of covering the most important use cases. If you have completly non-overlapping global use cases, teach your users to select and agent (or have an agent with different modes). You might also use the Orchestrator in this case, but it has some down sides if it does not work 100%
- If the context gets too large or performance degrades, the next step is to **extract some steps** into sub-agents or skills.
- **Which extraction mechanism works best**depends on the nature of what you're extracting:

- If it's a **separate, repeated workflow** with its own tools → lean toward a **sub-agent** (delegation)
- If it's a **capability that should be available throughout the whole session** → lean toward a **skill** or **capability**
Hope that gives you a useful overview! That said, it's really hard to give more concrete guidance without knowing your particular use case in detail — the "right" approach depends heavily on what your agents actually do, how their capabilities overlap, how complex the tasks are, and what your users expect. If you can share more specifics about your setup, we're happy to dig deeper.
Best,

_Your context window is not infinite. Subagents are how you stop treating it like it is — and start building AI workflows that actually scale._

![](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:700/1*y3TOZ8xOYnoy3ckduVlWfA.png)

Claude Code Subagents — A Complete Guide

Every developer who uses Claude Code long enough hits the same wall. The session starts fast. The first hour is productive. Then, somewhere around the third or fourth hour, something changes. Responses get vague. The model starts forgetting decisions made an hour ago. Code suggestions drift from the established patterns. The context window is full, and it is full of noise.

The standard response is to start a fresh session. But that means losing all the accumulated understanding — the file structure you explored, the architecture you discussed, the edge cases you already caught. You are trading away context to regain sharpness, and neither option is good.

Subagents are the architectural solution to this problem. They are not a convenience feature or a power-user shortcut. They are how Claude Code is designed to handle serious, long-running engineering work — by isolating noisy tasks in their own context windows so the main conversation stays clean. Subagents are the architectural solution to this problem. They are not a convenience feature or a power-user shortcut. They are how Claude Code is designed to handle serious, long-running engineering work — by isolating noisy tasks in their own context windows so the main conversation stays clean.

![](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:700/1*0KZrTCkMz752bFK9rTRDCQ.png)

## What a subagent actually is

A subagent in Claude Code is a named, isolated Claude instance with its own system prompt, its own context window, its own tool access list, and its own permission mode. When the main agent delegates a task to a subagent, the subagent runs independently, does its work, and returns only its final output to the parent. All the intermediate noise — the file reads, the search results, the exploratory tool calls — stays inside the subagent’s context and never touches the main conversation.

This is the real value, and it is worth being precise about: subagents do not make Claude smarter. They preserve the quality of the context that already exists. A 200K-token context window sounds enormous until you realize that a multi-hour session on a real codebase fills it with tool output, conversation history, and repeated file contents. Once you are at two-thirds capacity, response quality degrades — not because the model changed, but because the signal-to-noise ratio collapsed.

Press enter or click to view image in full size

![](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:700/1*9aPl4WNVzaBZumvM5x7ECg.png)

The three built-in subagents Claude Code ships with illustrate the design principle clearly. **Explore** is read-only and runs on Haiku by default — it is optimized for speed and cost, designed to search and understand a codebase without making changes. **Plan** gathers context before Claude presents a strategy in plan mode. **General-purpose** handles tasks that need both exploration and modification. You rarely invoke these directly; Claude routes to them automatically based on what you are asking.

Press enter or click to view image in full size

![](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:700/1*UkEp5H7h0uMUSjSoPs-Qcg.png)

## The anatomy of a subagent definition

Every subagent is a Markdown file with YAML frontmatter. The frontmatter is the configuration — it declares the agent’s name, when to use it, which tools it can access, which model it runs on, and what permissions it operates under. The Markdown body below the frontmatter is the system prompt — the instructions that define how the agent behaves when it runs.

**.claude/agents/security-reviewer.md**

```
---
name: security-reviewer
description: Security-focused code reviewer. Use proactively after writing
             authentication, authorization, or data-handling code. Also
             triggers on "check this for security issues" or "audit my auth".
tools: Read, Grep, Glob        # read-only — cannot modify files
model: opus                    # high-stakes review gets Opus
effort: high                   # max reasoning depth
permissionMode: default        # respects standard permission gates
---

You are a senior application security engineer. Your role is to review code
for security vulnerabilities before it ships.

When invoked:
1. Run `git diff HEAD` to see recent changes
2. Identify the highest-risk areas: auth flows, input handling, data exposure
3. Check for: SQL injection, XSS, IDOR, missing auth checks, secrets in code
4. Report findings as: CRITICAL / HIGH / MEDIUM / LOW with line references
5. Suggest the minimal fix for each finding — do not rewrite the code

Return a structured report. Do not modify any files.
```

The description field is doing the same work it does in a SKILL.md — it is the trigger, not the label. Claude matches the user’s request against subagent descriptions to decide whether to delegate automatically. Write it like a routing rule: describe the exact phrases and situations that should invoke this agent, including “use proactively” if you want Claude to reach for it without being asked.

**Complete frontmatter reference**

![](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:700/1*hPTeGdo0kuGsmsf5aFdzag.png)

## Where subagents live — and who can see them

Subagent files live in one of four locations, each with different scope and priority. When names collide, Claude Code resolves them in a strict order: session-defined agents win, then project agents, then user agents, then plugin agents.

Press enter or click to view image in full size

![](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:700/1*WeqIUj44IdIaRbG-VRzu2Q.png)

The practical rule: project-level agents (`.claude/agents/`) should define the team's shared specialists — the reviewer, the test runner, the documentation writer. These get committed to the repo so every engineer works with the same agent definitions. User-level agents (`~/.claude/agents/`) are personal tools you bring to every project — a coding style enforcer tuned to your preferences, or a research agent that accumulates knowledge about topics you care about over time.

```
# Interactive creation — recommended approach
/agents

# Then choose: Create new → Project scope → Generate with Claude
# Claude asks what the agent should do, generates the definition

# Or create manually at the right location
mkdir -p .claude/agents
touch .claude/agents/dependency-auditor.md

# After creating, verify it's visible
/agents
# Lists all agents: built-in, project, user, plugin
# Shows which is active when duplicates exist
```

## Three production-ready subagents

The fastest way to understand subagent design is to read real definitions. Here are three that cover common engineering patterns — a read-only auditor, a test specialist, and a dependency reviewer — each demonstrating a different set of trade-offs.

1. **Dependency auditor (read-only, safe to run anywhere)**

**.claude/agents/dependency-auditor.md**

```
---
name: dependency-auditor
description: Review dependencies and lockfiles for upgrade opportunities,
             security vulnerabilities, and supply-chain risks. Use when
             adding packages, before major releases, or on "audit deps".
tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash
disallowedTools: Edit, Write    # never modifies files
permissionMode: plan            # shows plan before any bash command
model: sonnet
isolation: true
---

You are a dependency security specialist. Audit this project's dependencies
and report findings. Never modify any files.

Steps:
1. Find package.json / requirements.txt / go.mod / Cargo.toml
2. Read lockfiles (package-lock.json, poetry.lock, etc.)
3. Check for: outdated major versions, known CVEs in package names,
   suspicious packages (typosquatting patterns), overly broad version ranges
4. For each finding: package name, current version, recommended version, risk

Format output as a table. Be specific. Do not suggest running npm install.
```

**2\. Test runner and fixer (controlled execution)**

**.claude/agents/test-runner.md**

```
---
name: test-runner
description: Run the test suite, isolate failures, and propose minimal fixes.
             Use proactively after code changes. Triggers on "run tests",
             "fix failing tests", or "make the tests pass".
tools: Read, Bash, Grep, Edit
model: sonnet
maxTurns: 20                    # cap iterations — tests can spiral
---

You are a test automation specialist. Your goal is a green test suite.

Workflow:
1. Run the test command (check package.json / Makefile for the right one)
2. Read failing test output carefully — identify the root failure, not symptoms
3. Trace the failure to the source file, not the test file
4. Make the minimal change to fix the root cause
5. Re-run tests to confirm
6. If you cannot fix in 3 attempts, report what you found and stop

Never delete tests to make them pass. Never skip assertions.
Report your fix with the line numbers changed.
```

**3\. Research agent with persistent memory**

**~/.claude/agents/researcher.md**

```
---
name: researcher
description: Long-running research assistant. Use for deep-dive questions
             about libraries, APIs, architecture patterns, or technical
             concepts. Accumulates knowledge across sessions via memory.
tools: Read, Bash, Glob, Grep
model: opus
effort: high
memory: user                   # persists to ~/.claude/agent-memory/researcher/
---

You are a technical researcher who remembers what you've investigated before.

When invoked:
1. Check your MEMORY.md for anything relevant to the current question
2. Do thorough research using your available tools
3. After answering, update MEMORY.md with: the question asked, key findings,
   sources consulted, and any follow-up questions that emerged

Keep MEMORY.md concise — prioritize findings over process.
Your accumulated knowledge makes you more useful over time.
```

![](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:700/1*T1euYt9mdHw7-JnrctHfUQ.png)

## The Explore → Plan → Execute pattern

The most reliable pattern for complex engineering tasks with subagents is a three-phase pipeline that mirrors how a careful engineer approaches an unfamiliar codebase. Each phase is a distinct subagent invocation, and each phase produces a clean handoff to the next.

Press enter or click to view image in full size

![](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:700/1*q5NKNslfZCzkQ_TUXAApqw.png)

The key insight is that the human review gate goes between Plan and Execute, not between Explore and Plan. Exploration is cheap — let the agent read freely. Planning is analytical — let the agent design the approach. But before you let any agent modify files, you want to see the plan and approve it. This is where plan mode (`permissionMode: plan`) earns its place: the Execute agent shows you exactly what it intends to do before touching anything.

**Claude.md**

```
## Agent Delegation Rules

### Explore-Plan-Execute pipeline
For ANY task that touches more than 3 files or involves refactoring:
1. First invoke the explore subagent to map the relevant files
2. Use its output to invoke the plan subagent with specific scope
3. Present the plan to the user for approval
4. Only then invoke execute with the approved plan as context

### Direct execution (no subagents)
- Quick targeted fixes (1 file, <20 lines)
- Changes to files already open in conversation context
- Tasks with frequent back-and-forth that need immediate feedback

### Domain routing
When implementing features that span domains, spawn parallel agents:
- Frontend (React/CSS): @frontend-agent
- Backend (API/DB):     @backend-agent
- Tests:               @test-runner (use proactively after any code change)
```

## Parallel vs sequential: when to use each

Not all tasks benefit from parallel subagents. The rule is dependency: if two tasks need each other’s output to proceed, they must be sequential. If they are truly independent, parallelise them. The overhead of launching a subagent is real — each one starts fresh and spends the first few turns rebuilding local understanding — so parallelizing four tasks that each take two minutes saves eight minutes; parallelising four tasks that each take thirty seconds costs more than it saves.

Press enter or click to view image in full size

![](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:700/1*HP_ME6TXNcLFUfYFBRtT0A.png)

## Model routing: the cost optimization most people miss

Every subagent can run on a different model. This is one of the most impactful optimizations in the entire subagent system, and it is the one most developers ignore because they do not realize it is an option.

The pattern that works: run your main session on Opus for high-level reasoning, architectural judgment, and synthesis. Route implementation work and routine searches to Sonnet. Route file discovery, simple lookups, and transformations to Haiku. The cost difference is significant — Haiku is roughly 15× cheaper per token than Opus — and on tasks that do not require deep reasoning, the quality difference is negligible.

```
# Set a default model for all subagents that use "inherit"
export CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL="claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929"

# Run main session on Opus, subagents default to Sonnet
# Individual subagent frontmatter can override this per-agent
claude --model claude-opus-4-6

# Result: Opus for coordination + judgment
#         Sonnet for implementation subagents
#         Haiku (set in frontmatter) for Explore / search agents
```

Press enter or click to view image in full size

![](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:700/1*P2Gk2U2lJPAWBSNac8msxg.png)

## Subagents vs Agent Teams: which to reach for

Subagents and Agent Teams solve related but distinct problems. Subagents work within a single session — they delegate focused tasks to isolated workers, and results flow back to the main agent. Agent Teams (currently experimental, enabled via `CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1`) coordinate multiple independent Claude Code sessions that can communicate directly with each other.

Press enter or click to view image in full size

![](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:700/1*cAnL5SWwYPg4E4MWTEYAtQ.png)

The practical decision: use subagents when workers do not need to communicate with each other. Use Agent Teams when your teammates need to share discoveries mid-task, challenge each other’s assumptions, or coordinate on cross-cutting changes. For most development tasks in 2026, subagents are the right answer — they are stable, well-understood, and the isolation model maps cleanly onto how engineers already think about task decomposition.

Press enter or click to view image in full size

![](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:700/1*VLKQmPcbpA8LOuNwqYfWSw.png)

## The shift this represents

Subagents are not a feature you add to your workflow. They are a change in how you conceptualize the relationship between a developer and an AI coding tool. The single-session, single-context model made sense when LLMs were novelties and context windows were small. As sessions get longer, codebases get larger, and tasks get more complex, the monolithic approach hits a wall that no amount of prompt engineering can fully compensate for.

The skill that matters in 2026 is not writing better prompts. It is knowing how to decompose work — identifying which tasks are self-contained, which outputs can be summarized cleanly, where the human review gates belong, and which specialist agent should own which domain. That is systems design applied to AI workflows. And it is exactly the kind of thinking that subagents are built to support.

Press enter or click to view image in full size

![](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:700/1*XgoW4fn4AQct6u48M4QglQ.png)
